article_title: Strategies for Postsecondary Students in Developmental Education
citation: Bailey, T., Bashford, J., Boatman, A., Squires, J., Weiss, M., Doyle, W., Valentine, J. C., LaSota, R., Polanin, J. R., Spinney, E., Wilson, W., Yeide, M., & Young, S. H. (2016). Strategies for postsecondary students in developmental education – A practice guide for college and university administrators, advisors, and faculty. Washington, DC: Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. http://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Use multiple measures—such as high school GPA alongside placement tests—to assess postsecondary readiness and place students
description: The guide recommends that institutions inform placement decisions with multiple measures rather than a single test, because measuring the imperfectly measured construct of college readiness in several ways improves measurement. It notes that adding information beyond the test itself can improve placement decisions and directs institutions to pilot and monitor alternative placement rubrics. The WWC rated this recommendation as having minimal supporting evidence.
requirements: Pilot alternative placement rubrics with existing administrative data and monitor effects on student outcomes over time
Secure faculty and staff buy-in by sharing error-rate research on single-test placement
constraints: Using multiple measures for placement is resource-intensive
target_learners: postsecondary students placed in or at risk of placement in developmental education
examples: Long Beach City College first offered alternative measures for placement in fall 2012 with 933 students and expanded over successive years
key_sources: Bailey, T., Bashford, J., Boatman, A., Squires, J., Weiss, M., Doyle, W., Valentine, J. C., LaSota, R., Polanin, J. R., Spinney, E., Wilson, W., Yeide, M., & Young, S. H. (2016). title: Require or incentivize regular participation in enhanced advising activities
description: Enhanced advising replaces quick, transactional advising with a holistic structure in which advisors ask deeper questions and engage more with students. The panel rated the evidence as moderate. Implementation typically requires reducing advisor-to-student ratios, which the guide notes are roughly 600:1 at large community colleges, and may be supported by technology-mediated advising tools that do not supplant direct advisor contact.
requirements: Reduce advisor-to-student ratios so advisors can engage holistically with students
constraints: Costs associated with reducing advisor-to-student ratios must be addressed
target_learners: postsecondary students in or at risk of developmental education
examples: In the Opening Doors program in Ohio, enhanced advising reduced the advisor-to-student ratio to 150:1, compared with the typical 1,000:1 in that college

title: Offer students performance-based monetary incentives
description: One of the guide's six recommendations is that institutions offer students performance-based monetary incentives, one of the structural interventions the panel identified. The guide includes budgeting guidance and implementation advice for this practice as part of creating conditions that give underprepared students the best chance of realizing their educational goals. The panel selected this practice from 21 initially considered practices after systematic evidence review.
requirements: Institutions must budget for the incentives, as reflected in the guide's guidance on how to budget for performance-based monetary incentives

title: Compress or mainstream developmental education with course redesign
description: The guide recommends compressing or mainstreaming developmental education through course redesign, an instructional intervention affecting the content and pacing of classroom instruction. Figure materials in the guide inventory acceleration strategies and planning issues for adopting compressed and mainstreaming models. The panel reviewed evidence on practices to accelerate, compress, or mainstream developmental education as one of its eight original practice areas.
requirements: Course redesign must be planned, as reflected in the guide's planning issues and considerations for adopting compressed and mainstreaming developmental education models
target_learners: postsecondary students placed in developmental education

title: Teach students how to become self-regulated learners
description: The guide recommends teaching self-regulated learning to students in developmental education, an instructional practice involving instructor and student roles across phases such as quiz reflection and guided self-reflection. The panel found little evidence for the broader practice area of teaching metacognition, productive persistence, and college success skills, and narrowed the recommendation accordingly. Sample materials include quizzes, reflection sheets, and paired discussion formats.
requirements: Instructors integrate self-regulated learning throughout a course using tools such as quizzes, reflection and revision sheets, and guided self-reflection
examples: The guide provides a sample self-regulated learning quiz in mathematics and a sample quiz reflection and revision sheet

title: Implement comprehensive, integrated, and long-lasting support programs
description: The guide's sixth recommendation is to implement comprehensive, integrated, and long-lasting support programs, illustrated by the Accelerated Study in Associate Programs. Unlike the other recommendations, this one involves a set of interdependent policies and practices that must operate together rather than in isolation. The guide notes such supports are among the bundles of interventions associated with relatively strong effects.
requirements: Interdependent policies and practices must be put in place at the same time
constraints: Unlike Recommendations 1–5, this practice cannot be implemented in isolation and depends on support of policymakers and administrators
target_learners: postsecondary students in or at risk of developmental education
examples: The guide presents postsecondary impacts of Accelerated Study in Associate Programs as an illustrative example

article_title: Using Bayesian Meta-Analysis to Explore the Components of Early Literacy Interventions. WWC 2023-008
citation: Elias Walsh, John Deke, Silvia Robles, Andrei Streke, and Dan Thal. (2023). Using Bayesian Meta-Analysis to Explore the Components of Early Literacy Interventions. What Works Clearinghouse, NCEE, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/Publication/WWC-2023008
title: WWC-reviewed study dataset of early literacy interventions (29 studies, 25 interventions, 22,596 students, 100 independent alphabetics findings)
description: The evidence base for the synthesis: high-quality studies drawn from the WWC's publicly available database of reviewed studies, all meeting WWC rigorous research standards and examining impacts on alphabetics outcomes in grades K-3. "The 29 studies examined the effectiveness of  25 distinct interventions and include 108 findings" on alphabetics outcomes; "The synthesis include s 100 of the 108 impact estimates" measured independently of study authors or intervention developers. The studies were conducted in five countries and "collectively included 22,596 students," spanning kindergarten through grade 3 and a wide range of student samples including English learners and students experiencing reading difficulty.
requirements: Studies must have been previously reviewed by the WWC and met WWC rigorous research standards
Findings must measure impacts on alphabetics outcomes
constraints: Findings may not generalize to all literacy interventions because some interventions have not been studied in designs meeting WWC standards, and the WWC has not exhaustively reviewed all literacy research
target_learners: K-3 students in the United States, Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom
target_learning_goals: alphabetics outcomes (phonics, phonemic awareness, phonological awareness, letter identification)
examples: A finding is defined as an impact estimate for a particular outcome measure and a particular sample within a study
key_sources: Elias Walsh, John Deke, Silvia Robles, Andrei Streke, and Dan Thal. (2023). Using Bayesian Meta-Analysis to Explore the Components of Early Literacy Interventions. What Works Clearinghouse, NCEE, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/Publication/WWC-2023008

article_title: Asymdystopia: The Threat of Small Biases in Evaluations of Education Interventions That Need to Be Powered to Detect Small Impacts
citation: John Deke, Thomas Wei, and Tim Kautz. (2018). Asymdystopia: The threat of small biases in evaluations of education interventions that need to be powered to detect small impacts. SREE Spring 2018 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: What Works Clearinghouse attrition bias model
description: A model used in federal evidence reviews including the What Works Clearinghouse (WWC 2013; 2014) for judging attrition bias in RCTs. It "assumes that attrition bias is ignorable so long as it accounts for less than 20 percent of whatever size impact is deemed substantively important." The authors apply it, with WWC data on attrition from more than 800 prior studies, to explore when attrition stops being acceptable as studies target smaller impacts.
requirements: Requires a judgment of what size impact is deemed substantively important
constraints: The model's ignorability assumption was calibrated for studies powered to detect impacts of 0.20 SD or larger
target_learning_goals: assessing attrition bias in randomized controlled trials
examples: Applied to WWC data on attrition from more than 800 prior studies to examine feasibility of lower attrition in future small-impact studies
key_sources: John Deke, Thomas Wei, and Tim Kautz. (2018). Asymdystopia: The threat of small biases in evaluations of education interventions that need to be powered to detect small impacts. SREE Spring 2018 Conference Abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED591611

article_title: Climbing up the Leaderboard: An Empirical Study of Applying Gamification Techniques to a Computer Programming Class
citation: Fotaris P, Mastoras T, Leinfellner R and Rosunally Y. (2016). Climbing Up the Leaderboard: An Empirical Study of Applying Gamification Techniques to a Computer Programming Class. The Electronic Journal of e-Learning Volume 14 Issue 2, pp94-110. www.ejel.org
title: Classroom version of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire? for collaborative Python revision
description: An open-source implementation of the TV quiz show used as the revision seminar format: teams of 4-5 contestants answered 15 increasingly difficult multiple-choice questions on Python, using lifelines (Poll The Class, 50/50, Ask A Friend), with guaranteed prize levels and cumulative team points on a Blackboard leaderboard. The article states the game "requires students to compare and discuss their answers with their teammates in ord er to come to a consensus regarding the answer, thus improving communication efficiency". Questions were created by instructors by editing a simple text file, and the game was made available for download weekly for self-assessment.
requirements: Teams must remain constant for the course duration
Non-team students must put away note-taking materials when quiz questions overlap with graded assessments
Games limited to 20 minutes so all teams play each seminar
constraints: Scoring was done manually by faculty each week
The authors note limited question and answer length made authoring challenging
target_learners: undergraduate computing students in revision seminars
examples: After twelve seminars the leading team won the title of Pythonista of the year and received chocolate bars; all answers were reviewed with the whole class as the game proceeded
key_sources: Fotaris P, Mastoras T, Leinfellner R and Rosunally Y. (2016). Climbing Up the Leaderboard: An Empirical Study of Applying Gamification Techniques to a Computer Programming Class. The Electronic Journal of e-Learning Volume 14 Issue 2, pp94-110. www.ejel.org. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1101229

article_title: Valuing a More Rigorous Review of Formative Assessment's Effectiveness
citation: Apthorp, H., Klute, M., Petrites, T., Harlacher, J., & Reale, M. (2016). Valuing a more rigorous review of formative assessment's effectiveness. SREE Spring 2016 Conference Proposal. https://www.relcentral.org/news-and-events/the-essence-of-formative-assessment-creating-a-common-understanding-of-the-formative-assessment-process/
title: WWC-modeled three-level evidence rating system for formative assessment studies
description: The review assigned evidence ratings "using an approach modeled after the What Works Clearinghouse (WWC) Procedures and Standards Handbook, Version 3.0, for reviewing comparative group designs". WWC-certified researchers rated each eligible study into one of three categories: meets standards without reservations (highest, supporting causal inference), meets standards with reservations (does not support attribution of cause solely to formative assessment), and does not meet standards (not rigorous enough to support causal interpretation). Coding used a form adapted from McMillan et al. (2013).
requirements: Studies must be comparative group designs reviewable under WWC Version 3.0 procedures, with WWC-certified researchers completing the WWC Study Review Guide
constraints: Studies rated does not meet standards were not rigorous enough to support the interpretation that a formative assessment intervention caused the reported results
target_learning_goals: establishing causal evidence for formative assessment effectiveness
examples: The review screened over 160,000 identified studies through three additional screening phases, yielding 152 studies eligible for rigorous review and rating
key_sources: Apthorp, H., Klute, M., Petrites, T., Harlacher, J., & Reale, M. (2016). Valuing a more rigorous review of formative assessment's effectiveness. SREE Spring 2016 Conference Proposal. https://www.relcentral.org/news-and-events/the-essence-of-formative-assessment-creating-a-common-understanding-of-the-formative-assessment-process/

article_title: Improving Post-High School Outcomes for Transition-Age Students with Disabilities: An Evidence Review. NCEE 2013-4011
citation: Cobb, R. B., Lipscomb, S., Wolgemuth, J., Schulte, T., Veliquette, A., Alwell, M., Batchelder, K., Bernard, R., Hernandez, P., Holmquist-Johnson, H., Orsi, R., Sample McMeeking, L., Wang, J., and Weinberg, A. (2013). Improving Post-High School Outcomes for Transition-Age Students with Disabilities: An Evidence Review (NCEE 2013-4011). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. http://ies.ed.gov/pubsearch/pubsinfo.asp?pubid=NCEE20134011
title: What Works Clearinghouse evidence standards and reporting indicators applied to transition research
description: The review applies the WWC Procedures and Standards Handbook, Version 2.1, including pilot single-case design standards, to rate transition studies. Reporting indicators include the rating of effectiveness (positive, potentially positive, mixed, no discernible, potentially negative, or negative effects), the improvement index (percentile-point change for an average student), and the extent of evidence rating (small versus medium-to-large, based on number of studies, schools, and participants). SCDs contribute evidence only when at least five studies from three distinct research teams with at least 20 participants meet pilot standards.
requirements: Two WWC-certified reviewers independently review each study with reconciliation
Reliable outcome measures free of measurement problems
constraints: All studies with the same rating are treated equally regardless of sample size
WWC has no method for combining evidence across SCD studies
The review process did not directly assess implementation fidelity
examples: An improvement index of +10 indicates a comparison-group student at the 50th percentile would improve to the 60th percentile after participating.

B., Lipscomb, S., Wolgemuth, J., Schulte, T., Veliquette, A., Alwell, M., Batchelder, K., Bernard, R., Hernandez, P., Holmquist-Johnson, H., Orsi, R., Sample McMeeking, L., Wang, J., and Weinberg, A.
